title: Physics in 2-Steps: Locking Motion Priors Before Visual Refinement Erases Them
claim: Few-step outputs keep correct motion but lose detail while many-step outputs look good but break physics; ours gets both.
layout: 2 panels: tradeoff scatter left, three video strips right, arrows linking points
description: The left panel is a scatter plot with Physics Score on the x-axis (bad to good) and Visual Quality on the y-axis (low to high). A blue dot marks Step=50, which has high visual quality but low physics. A red dot marks Step=2, which has low quality but moderate physics. A green star marked Ours sits in a shaded green region at the top right. A black arrow runs from the red dot to the star. On the right, three colour-coded video strips of four frames each show a dropped ball and block. The blue strip, Baseline (Step 50), has a blue X and shows hallucinated motion. The red strip, Baseline (Step 2), is blurry but shows correct falling motion, marked by a lock icon. The green strip, Ours, is sharp and physically correct. A pink Motion Prior arrow points up from the red strip to the green strip. White arrows mark the motion. Shaded cones link each plot point to its strip. At the top, a dashed box holds the input image and text prompt.
caption: Overview of \model. Few-step inference ($T=2$) captures accurate physical motion (following the white arrow) but lacks textural detail, whereas standard inference ($T=50$) achieves photorealism but compromises physical integrity with hallucinations. Our method, \model, extracts the valid motion prior from the few-step inference stage and injects it during the denoising steps, improving physical consistency while largely preserving visual fidelity. Sec. [ref] details the specific experimental setup.
abstract: Image-to-Video diffusion models leverage input images to generate visually stunning content, yet frequently produce motion that violates physical laws. We reveal a surprising finding: a 2-step generation often exhibits better physical consistency than a 50-step output from the same model. Through spectral analysis, we trace this to phase erosion during denoising; the phase degrades significantly (dropping by $\approx 18\%$ from step 2 to step 50), whereas the magnitude remains relatively stable. Building on this insight, we propose PhaseLock, a training-free framework that preserves the valid motion priors from few-step inference throughout the denoising trajectory. Rather than relying on full-step inference for physical consistency, PhaseLock extracts a motion prior from just 2 steps and enforces it onto high-fidelity generation via Latent Delta Guidance. Our approach effectively mitigates phase degradation, improving physical consistency by an average of 6.2 points across diverse models while largely maintaining visual fidelity, with negligible overhead ($1.06\times$ time, $1.02\times$ memory) and reduced reliance on expensive external guidance methods ($\sim5\times$ time). Project Page: https://dnwjddl.github.io/phaselock
